prompt: What explains the overall shape of the periodic table?

choices.text: The shape mimics the way electrons fill the shells and subshells of atoms.
Elements are arranged by atomic mass, and each row holds elements of similar mass.
choices.why: The elements are listed by atomic number, and the shape comes from the order in which subshells fill with electrons, not from mass.

choices.text: Metals are gathered on the left side and nonmetals on the right side.
choices.why: Finding metals and nonmetals is one use of the table, but it doesn't explain the table's shape; the blocks match the subshells being filled.

choices.text: Every row holds the same number of elements, one for each electron a shell can hold.
choices.why: The rows are not all the same length; the first row has only two elements. Each row's length follows the subshells being filled across it.

explanation: The shape of the periodic table mimics the filling of subshells with electrons. Each section of the table (each block) matches the type of subshell being filled there: s, p, d, or f.

prompt: The first row of the periodic table holds only two elements, H and He. Why so few?

choices.text: The n = 1 shell has only the 1s subshell, which holds at most two electrons.
The n = 1 shell has a 1s and a 1p subshell, but the 1p subshell stays empty.
choices.why: There is no 1p subshell. The n = 1 shell has only an s subshell, so it is full after two electrons.

choices.text: Every shell can hold a maximum of two electrons.
choices.why: Only the n = 1 shell is limited to two electrons, because it has just one subshell. Higher shells have more subshells, such as p subshells, and hold more electrons.

choices.text: Only H and He have their valence electrons in an s subshell.
choices.why: Many elements, such as Li and Na, also have their valence electrons in an s subshell. The first row is short because the n = 1 shell contains only one subshell.

explanation: H is 1s^1 and He is 1s^2. The 1s subshell is the only subshell in the n = 1 shell, and an s subshell holds a maximum of two electrons, so with He the n = 1 shell is filled and the row ends.

prompt: Ne is the last element in the second row of the periodic table. Why does the next element, Na, start a new row instead of continuing the second row?

choices.text: Ne fills the n = 2 shell, so Na's last electron goes into the 3s subshell.
Na's last electron goes into a 2d subshell, which begins a new row.
choices.why: The n = 2 shell has only an s and a p subshell; there is no 2d subshell.

choices.text: Na's last electron goes into the 3p subshell, which begins a new row.
choices.why: The 3s subshell is filled before 3p. Na and Mg fill 3s; the 3p subshell is filled by the elements after them in the same row.

choices.text: Na's last electron goes into the 2s subshell, which begins a new row.
choices.why: The 2s subshell was already filled by Be. By Ne, every subshell in the n = 2 shell is full.

explanation: Ne fills the 2p subshell, completing the n = 2 shell. Na's 11th electron must go into the n = 3 shell, starting with the 3s subshell, so Na begins the third row, back on the left side of the table where s subshells are filled.

prompt: In the second row, B comes right after Be, yet B sits on the right side of the periodic table, far from Be. Why?

choices.text: B's last electron starts the 2p subshell, and p subshells are filled on the right side.
B's last electron goes into the 2s subshell, which is filled on the right side.
choices.why: The 2s subshell is filled on the left side of the table, and it is already full at Be.

choices.text: B's last electron starts the 2p subshell, which is filled in the middle of the table.
choices.why: The middle section of the table is the d block, where d subshells are filled. The p subshells are filled on the right side.

choices.text: The space between Be and B is saved for second-row elements filling a 2d subshell.
choices.why: There is no 2d subshell; the n = 2 shell has only s and p subshells, so no second-row elements belong in the middle section.

explanation: Be completes the 2s subshell, which is filled in the first two columns on the left. B's next electron starts the 2p subshell, and p subshells are filled in the p block on the right side of the table, so B is placed there.

prompt: The n = 3 shell has a 3d subshell, yet none of the third-row elements (Na through Ar) are in the middle section of the periodic table, where d subshells are filled. Why not?

choices.text: Electrons fill 4s before 3d, so 3d is filled in the fourth row.
The n = 3 shell can hold only eight electrons, so it is full at Ar.
choices.why: The 3d subshell can take up to 10 more electrons; they simply arrive later, after the 4s subshell has been filled.

choices.text: The 3d subshell is filled only after the 4p subshell.
choices.why: The 3d subshell is filled before 4p. Only the 4s subshell comes ahead of 3d.

choices.text: The 3d subshell is filled in the f block, drawn below the main table.
choices.why: The f block is where f subshells are filled. A d subshell is filled in the d block, the middle section of the table.

explanation: Instead of filling the 3d subshell after 3p, electrons go into the 4s subshell. Only after 4s is filled does the 3d subshell fill, so the 3d elements appear in the middle section of the fourth row, not the third.

prompt: How many elements are in the second row of the periodic table?
explanation: Across the second row, electrons fill the 2s subshell (at most 2 electrons) and then the 2p subshell (at most 6 electrons). Each element adds one electron, so the row has 2 + 6 = 8 elements.

prompt: The f block is the section of the periodic table that is normally drawn detached from the main body. How many columns wide is the f block?
explanation: The f block is a 14-column section. Its elements are filling f subshells, which hold up to 14 electrons.

prompt: Why is the f block usually drawn as a separate section below the main body of the periodic table?

choices.text: It could be part of the main body, but then the table would be long and cumbersome.
Its elements do not follow the pattern of subshells filling with electrons.
choices.why: The f-block elements follow the same pattern: they are the elements filling f subshells. Drawing them separately is only a matter of convenience.

choices.text: Its elements are not arranged in order of atomic number.
choices.why: Like the rest of the table, the f block is in order of atomic number; it would slot into the main body if the table were drawn wider.

choices.text: Its elements are filling d subshells that don't fit in the middle section.
choices.why: The elements filling d subshells are in the d block, the middle section. The f block is where f subshells are being filled.

explanation: The f block holds the elements filling f subshells. It could be part of the main body of the periodic table, but then the table would be rather long and cumbersome, so it is normally drawn detached.

prompt: Which of these elements is in the s block of the periodic table?

choices.text: K, [Ar]4s^1

choices.why: Hg has 6s^2, but the last subshell being filled is 5d, so Hg is in the d block.

choices.text: Al, [Ne]3s^2 3p^1
choices.why: Al's last electron is in the 3p subshell, so Al is in the p block.
O is filling the 2p subshell, so it is in the p block, even though its configuration includes 2s^2.

explanation: An element's block depends on which subshell is being filled. K's last electron goes into the 4s subshell, so K is in the s block (its first column). The others are filling 5d, 3p, and 2p subshells.

prompt: An element has the electron configuration [Kr]5s^2 4d^10 5p^1. Where is it on the periodic table?

choices.text: Fifth row, first column of the p block
Fifth row, third column of the p block
choices.why: This counts the 5s electrons too. Within the p block, the column number is the number of p electrons, and there is one (5p^1).

choices.text: Fourth row, first column of the p block
choices.why: The configuration includes 4d^10, but its highest-numbered shell is n = 5, so the element is in the fifth row.

choices.text: Fifth row, last column of the d block
choices.why: The 4d subshell is already full. The last subshell being filled is 5p, which puts the element in the p block.

explanation: The last subshell being filled is 5p, so the element is in the p block; one 5p electron puts it in the first column of that block; and its valence shell is n = 5, so it is in the fifth row. (This is indium, In.)

prompt: An element is in the sixth row of the periodic table, in the third column of the p block. How should its electron configuration end?

choices.why: In the sixth row, the p subshell being filled is 6p. The 5p subshell is filled in the fifth row.
This treats the column number as the total number of valence electrons (6s^2 6p^1). Within the p block, the column number is the number of p electrons.
The d subshells are filled in the middle d block. An element in the p block has a configuration ending in a p subshell.

explanation: An element in the p block has a configuration ending in p, and its column within the block gives the number of p electrons. In the sixth row the p subshell is 6p, so the configuration should end in 6p^3. (This is bismuth, Bi.)

prompt: Yttrium (Y) is in the fifth row of the periodic table, in the first column of the d block. A student predicts that its electron configuration is [Kr]5s^2 5d^1. What is the student's mistake?

choices.text: The d subshell filled in the fifth row is 4d, so it should be [Kr]5s^2 4d^1.
The core should be [Ar], so it should be [Ar]5s^2 5d^1.
choices.why: Kr is the noble gas at the end of the fourth row, so [Kr] is the right core for a fifth-row element.

choices.text: A d-block element ends in p, so it should be [Kr]5s^2 5p^1.
choices.why: A configuration ends in p only for p-block elements. In the d block, a d subshell is being filled.

choices.text: The 5s subshell isn't filled yet, so it should be [Kr]5d^1.
choices.why: The two s-block elements at the start of the fifth row fill 5s before the d block begins, so 5s^2 belongs in the configuration.

explanation: In the fifth row, the middle d block fills the 4d subshell, after the 5s subshell. The first column of the d block has one d electron, so yttrium's expected configuration is [Kr]5s^2 4d^1.

prompt: Bromine (Br) is in the fourth row of the periodic table, in the fifth column of the p block. A student writes its electron configuration as [Ar]4s^2 4p^5. What is wrong?

choices.text: It leaves out the filled 3d subshell; it should be [Ar]4s^2 3d^10 4p^5.
It leaves out a filled 4d subshell; it should be [Ar]4s^2 4d^10 4p^5.
choices.why: A d subshell does fill between 4s and 4p, but in the fourth row it is 3d, not 4d.

choices.text: The core should be [Kr], so it should be [Kr]4s^2 4p^5.
choices.why: Kr ends the fourth row, after Br. A fourth-row element uses the core of the noble gas that ends the third row, Ar.

choices.text: The p electrons belong in 3p, so it should be [Ar]4s^2 3p^5.
choices.why: The 3p subshell is already full inside the [Ar] core. In the fourth row, the p block fills 4p.

explanation: In the fourth row, the 3d subshell is filled (in the d block) after 4s and before 4p, so a fourth-row p-block element has a full 3d subshell: Br is [Ar]4s^2 3d^10 4p^5.

prompt: Manganese (Mn) is in the fourth row of the periodic table, in the fifth column of the d block. Which electron configuration does its position predict?

choices.why: In the fourth row, the d block fills the 3d subshell, not 4d.
The 4s subshell fills before 3d, so Mn's configuration includes 4s^2.
That would be the fifth column of the d block in the fifth row. Mn is in the fourth row, so its core is [Ar].

explanation: A fourth-row element has an [Ar] core and fills 4s first. The d block in the fourth row fills 3d, and the fifth column means five d electrons: [Ar]4s^2 3d^5.

prompt: Which position on the periodic table belongs to an element whose electron configuration is expected to end in 6s^2?

choices.text: Sixth row, second column of the s block
Sixth row, first column of the s block
choices.why: The first column of the s block has one s electron, so its configuration ends in 6s^1.

choices.text: Fifth row, second column of the s block
choices.why: In the fifth row, the s subshell being filled is 5s, so this element's configuration ends in 5s^2.

choices.text: Sixth row, second column of the p block
choices.why: An element in the p block has a configuration ending in a p subshell, here 6p^2.

explanation: An s^2 ending means the second column of the s block, and the 6s subshell is filled in the sixth row. (This is barium, [Xe]6s^2.)

prompt: An element is in the third row of the periodic table, in the fourth column of the p block. How many valence electrons does an atom of this element have?
explanation: Its configuration should end in 3s^2 3p^4 (it is S, [Ne]3s^2 3p^4). Both the 3s and 3p electrons are in the highest-numbered shell, n = 3, so it has 2 + 4 = 6 valence electrons.

prompt: Lead (Pb), atomic number 82, has the electron configuration [Xe]6s^2 4f^14 5d^10 6p^2. How many valence electrons does a Pb atom have?
explanation: The highest-numbered shell is n = 6, which holds 6s^2 6p^2, or 4 electrons. The 4f and 5d subshells are full and belong to lower shells, so their electrons are core electrons.

prompt: Iodine (I), atomic number 53, has the electron configuration [Kr]5s^2 4d^10 5p^5. How many core electrons does an iodine atom have?
explanation: The valence electrons are the 7 in the highest-numbered shell, n = 5 (5s^2 5p^5). All the rest are core electrons: 36 in the [Kr] core plus 10 in the filled 4d subshell, or 53 − 7 = 46.

prompt: Rhenium (Re), atomic number 75, has the electron configuration [Xe]6s^2 4f^14 5d^5. Counting valence electrons as this section defines them, how many valence electrons does a Re atom have?
explanation: Valence electrons are the electrons in the highest-numbered shell plus any in the last unfilled subshell. Re has 2 in the n = 6 shell (6s^2) and 5 in the unfilled 5d subshell, so 2 + 5 = 7. The full 4f subshell holds core electrons.

prompt: A student says that silicon, [Ne]3s^2 3p^2, has only two valence electrons, because its 3s subshell is full and only the 3p subshell is unfilled. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: All electrons in the highest-numbered shell are valence electrons, giving four.
The 10 electrons of the [Ne] core count as valence electrons too, giving 12.
choices.why: The [Ne] electrons are inner electrons. They are core electrons, not valence electrons.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: only electrons in unfilled subshells are valence electrons.
choices.why: All the electrons in the highest-numbered shell count, whether their subshell is full or not, and the 3s electrons are in the n = 3 shell.

choices.text: The 3p electrons are core electrons, so only the two 3s electrons count.
choices.why: The 3p subshell is in the n = 3 shell, the valence shell, so its electrons are valence electrons.

explanation: Valence electrons are the electrons in the highest-numbered shell, plus any in the last unfilled subshell. For Si the highest-numbered shell is n = 3, so both 3s electrons and both 3p electrons count: 4 valence electrons.

prompt: Why do elements in the same column of the periodic table have similar chemical properties?

choices.text: They have the same valence shell electron configuration.
They have the same number of core electrons.
choices.why: Core electrons increase going down a column: Li has 2, Na has 10, and K has 18.

choices.text: They have the same total number of electrons.
choices.why: Each element has a different atomic number, so the elements in a column have different numbers of electrons.

choices.text: They are either all metals or all nonmetals.
choices.why: Some columns hold both metals and nonmetals. What the elements in a column share is their valence shell electron configuration.

explanation: Elements in a column have the same valence shell electron configuration; for example, H, Li, Na, K, Rb, and Cs each have a single s electron in their valence shell. Because valence electrons largely control an atom's chemistry, these elements behave similarly.

prompt: N (atomic number 7) and P (atomic number 15) are in the same column of the periodic table. What do their electron configurations have in common?

choices.text: Both have an s^2 p^3 valence shell configuration.
Both have their valence electrons in the n = 2 shell.
choices.why: P is one row lower than N, so its valence shell is n = 3.

choices.text: Both have the same number of core electrons.
choices.why: N has 2 core electrons (1s^2), while P has 10 (the [Ne] core).

choices.text: Both have only three valence electrons, the ones in the p subshell.
choices.why: The s electrons in the valence shell are valence electrons too, so each has five.

explanation: Elements in the same column share the same valence shell configuration. N is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3 and P is [Ne]3s^2 3p^3, so both have s^2 p^3 in their valence shell, in the n = 2 and n = 3 shells.

prompt: Based on their electron configurations, which pair of elements would you expect to have similar chemistry?

choices.text: S, [Ne]3s^2 3p^4, and Cl, [Ne]3s^2 3p^5
choices.why: S and Cl are neighbors in the same row. Their valence shells differ (3s^2 3p^4 versus 3s^2 3p^5), so they are in different columns.

choices.text: Mg, [Ne]3s^2, and Al, [Ne]3s^2 3p^1
choices.why: Both have 3s^2, but Al also has a 3p electron, so their valence shell configurations differ and they are in different columns.
They share the [Ar] core and the filled 3d subshell, but those are core electrons. Their valence shells differ (4s^2 4p^4 versus 4s^2 4p^2).

explanation: Elements with the same valence shell configuration are in the same column and have similar chemistry. S (3s^2 3p^4) and Se (4s^2 4p^4) both have an s^2 p^4 valence shell, just in different shells.

prompt: Elements in the same column of the periodic table have the same valence shell electron configuration. In which blocks is this strictly true?

choices.text: The s and p blocks
The d and f blocks
choices.why: These are the blocks where it is not absolute, because some of their elements are exceptions to the order of filling subshells.

choices.text: All four blocks, with no exceptions
choices.why: In the d and f blocks there are exceptions to the order of filling, so the match is not absolute there.

choices.text: Only the s block
choices.why: It is strictly true in the p block as well.

explanation: For the s and p blocks, every element in a column has the same valence shell configuration. In the d and f blocks, exceptions to the order of filling mean the match is not absolute, though many similarities still exist.

prompt: Ag (atomic number 47) is in the d block. From its position, its expected electron configuration is [Kr]5s^2 4d^9, but experiments show that it is actually [Kr]5s^1 4d^10. Which statement best describes this?

choices.text: Ag is an exception to the filling order; such exceptions occur in the d block.
Ag must belong in the s block, because its configuration has a single 5s electron.
choices.why: Ag stays in the d block, where a d subshell is being filled. An exception changes the configuration, not the element's place in the table.

choices.text: The experiment must be wrong, because position always gives the actual configuration.
choices.why: Experiments show the actual configuration. Position gives the expected one, and in the d and f blocks some elements are exceptions.

choices.text: No configuration in the d block can be predicted from position.
choices.why: Predictions from position still work for many d-block elements; they just aren't guaranteed in the d and f blocks, because some elements, like Ag, are exceptions.

explanation: Exceptions to the order of filling subshells occur in the d and f blocks, so an element's position gives its expected configuration, which is not always its actual one. Ag is one such exception; its place in the d block doesn't change.

prompt: Why does a ripe tomato look red?

choices.text: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colors in white light.
It absorbs red light and reflects the other colors in white light.
choices.why: This is backward. An object shows the color it reflects, so a red tomato reflects red light and absorbs the rest.

choices.text: It gives off its own red light, as a neon light does.
choices.why: Colored lights such as neon produce their own colors, but objects get their color a different way: by preferentially reflecting one color of the light that shines on them.

choices.text: It reflects every color of white light equally.
choices.why: An object is colored because it reflects one color preferentially. Reflecting every color equally wouldn't single out red.

explanation: Objects are colored because they preferentially reflect a certain color of the white light that shines on them. A red tomato reflects red light while absorbing all the other colors of the rainbow.

prompt: The d block of the periodic table is 10 columns wide. Why 10?

choices.text: A d subshell holds up to 10 electrons, and each column adds one d electron.
Every element in the d block has 10 valence electrons.
choices.why: The number of d electrons rises by one per column, from d^1 in the first column of the block to d^10 in the last.

choices.text: Each column fills a different d subshell, from 1d through 10d.
choices.why: There are no 1d or 2d subshells. Across a single row, all 10 columns of the d block are filling the same d subshell.

choices.text: Ten different shells contain a d subshell, one for each column.
choices.why: The 10 is the number of electrons one d subshell can hold, not a number of shells.

explanation: A d subshell can hold a maximum of 10 electrons. Across a row of the d block, each element adds one more electron to the same d subshell, so the block is 10 columns wide.

prompt: Calcium (Ca), atomic number 20, is in the fourth row of the periodic table, in the second column of the s block. What is the atomic number of the element in the fourth row, first column of the p block?
explanation: After Ca fills 4s, the next 10 elements (atomic numbers 21 through 30) fill the 3d subshell in the d block. The first p-block element of the row comes next: 20 + 10 + 1 = 31.

prompt: Na and Cl are both in the third row of the periodic table. Which statement about them is correct?

choices.text: Both have the n = 3 shell as their valence shell.
Both have the same valence shell electron configuration.
choices.why: Na's valence shell is 3s^1 and Cl's is 3s^2 3p^5, which are different.

choices.text: Both have the same number of valence electrons.
choices.why: Na has one valence electron (3s^1), while Cl has seven (3s^2 3p^5).

choices.text: Both are in the same block, because both have electrons in the 3s subshell.
choices.why: The block depends on the subshell being filled: Na is filling 3s (s block), but Cl is filling 3p (p block).

explanation: Na ([Ne]3s^1) and Cl ([Ne]3s^2 3p^5) both have n = 3 as their highest-numbered shell, which matches their place in the third row. Their valence shell configurations, and their numbers of valence electrons, are different.

prompt: One element has the electron configuration [Ne]3s^2 3p^2, and another has [Ar]4s^2 3d^2. A student notices that both end with two electrons in the last subshell and concludes that the two elements are in the same column. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: They are in different columns: the first is in the p block and the second is in the d block.
They are in the same column, because both end with two electrons in the last subshell.
choices.why: The first is filling a p subshell and the second a d subshell, so they are in different blocks, and so in different columns.

choices.text: They are in the same row, because both end with electrons in an n = 3 subshell.
choices.why: The row matches the highest-numbered shell: n = 3 for the first element but n = 4 (4s^2) for the second, so they are in the third and fourth rows.

choices.text: They are in different columns: the first is in the d block and the second is in the p block.
choices.why: This has the blocks reversed. The first is filling 3p (p block), and the second is filling 3d (d block).

explanation: An element's block depends on the subshell being filled. The first element (Si) is filling 3p, putting it in the p block; the second (Ti) is filling 3d, putting it in the d block. Different blocks means different columns, whatever the superscripts.
